title: New Product Development for Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky new product development works: stage gates, the aged stock constraint, liquid and pack development, state registrations and launch timing.
teaser: In most categories you design a product and then make it. In whisky the liquid had to be made years before anyone had the idea.
standfirst: Whisky NPD follows the same stage gates as any consumer product, with one big difference: the liquid is limited by what is already maturing in the warehouse. This guide walks through the process for brand, planning and finance teams.
sections:
A new soft drink can be formulated, tested and in production within months. A new whisky cannot, because its key ingredient is time. Scotch must mature for at least three years in oak casks in Scotland. A 12 year old expression needs spirit distilled at least twelve years before the bottle is filled.

So whisky NPD starts with a question most categories never ask: what do we already have in the warehouse? The answer decides which ideas are possible this year and which have to wait for stock laid down today. Our guide to what a new distillery sells while whisky ages shows the same constraint from the start-up side.

Most drinks companies run NPD through stage gates, with a decision at each.

  1. Idea and opportunity. A gap in a price tier, an occasion or a state. The consumer insight and a rough size of prize.
  2. Concept. A one page description, a working name, a price point and consumer testing of the concept.
  3. Liquid and pack development. The blender builds prototypes from available stock. Design develops the bottle, label and carton.
  4. Business case. Cost of goods, excise and pricing by state, volume forecast and capital needs such as new moulds or change parts.
  5. Launch readiness. Registrations, approvals, dry goods ordered, bottling trials and sales training.
  6. Launch and review. A post-launch review at an agreed point, often six or twelve months.
Liquid development is a stock question

The blender's job in NPD is to hit a target flavour profile from casks that exist and are not already promised to core brands. A brief that asks for a richer, fruitier whisky might be met with more sherry cask malt. If that stock is earmarked for the flagship, the blender has to find another route or the launch waits.

That is why liquid development runs alongside stock planning. A new expression that sells well can drain casks the core range needs in five years. Our guide to how limited edition whiskies are planned covers how teams protect core stock.
Pack development has long lead times

A new bottle shape needs a new glass mould, sampling and line trials. A new closure or premium gift box has its own supplier lead time. Labels for Indian whisky must be designed for each state where the product will be sold, because label content and approvals differ by state.

For the production team, a new pack means change parts on the filler, capper and labeller, trial runs and new specifications. A whisky line that handles 750, 375 and 180 ml bottles may need a whole new set of parts for an unusual shape.

Before a whisky can be sold in an Indian state, its label usually has to be registered and its price approved by the state excise department. That is a separate process in each state, often tied to the state's excise year. A launch planned for October can slip months if registration windows are missed.

Price tier decides much of the business case, because many states set duty in slabs by declared price. A product priced just above a slab boundary can pay noticeably more tax than one just below it. Rules vary by state and change, so the regulatory team should work from the current notification.

• The liquid needs stock that is already committed to core brands.
  • The pack is approved before the bottling line has trialled it.
  • The forecast includes pipeline fill as if it were repeat demand.
  • Registrations are planned for one state and the sales plan assumes ten.
  • The launch date is set before dry goods lead times are known.

None of these are creative failures. All of them are planning failures that a cross-functional team can catch at the right gate.

Take one idea your brand team is discussing and ask the blending or stock planning team two questions. What age and cask type would this need? How many litres of alcohol of it are free over the next three years? Their answers will tell you whether the idea is a launch, a limited edition or a plan for the future.
faqs: Why does whisky NPD take so long?
The liquid must already be maturing. An aged expression depends on spirit distilled years earlier, so ideas are limited by the stock that exists.
Who develops the liquid for a new whisky?
The blender builds prototypes from available casks against the brief, working with stock planning so core brands are not starved.
Why do whisky launches in India slip?
Label registration and price approval are needed state by state, often tied to the excise year. Missing a window or a dry goods lead time can delay a launch by months.
